# Part XI: Practice and Operations {#part-practice .unnumbered}

> "A complex system that works is invariably found to have evolved from a simple
> system that works."
>
> John Gall, ["Systemantics"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systemantics)

The last substantive part changes posture. Part IX exposed the physical and
frontier limits underneath the stack; Part X showed how those limits become
markets, openness choices, adoption patterns, and data-rights bargains. This
part asks how a team should wire the stack together and keep it alive. The work
is no longer only to trace mechanisms. It is to make choices under deadlines,
budgets, licenses, reliability targets, changing model releases, and production
incidents.

@sec-choosing-model starts with the first practical fork: rent a frontier model,
run an open one, or keep both options alive. @sec-serving-stack, @sec-edge, and
@sec-training-practice turn that choice into serving engines, gateways, compute,
edge deployments, and fine-tuning decisions. @sec-agents-practice and
@sec-retrieval-practice bring in frameworks, sandboxes, MCP, document parsing,
retrieval, and extraction. @sec-eval-practice and @sec-wiring-stack connect those
pieces with evaluations, observability, budgets, and a reference architecture for
a 2026 stack. @sec-deployment-lifecycle, @sec-reliability,
@sec-human-interface-oversight, @sec-data-engine, and @sec-operating-contracts
then cover the long tail: promotion, rollback, nondeterministic reliability,
human review surfaces, approval gates, production data, SLOs, cost governance,
incidents, multi-tenancy, and the loop that turns failures into better tests.

This part is not a recipe to copy once. It is a way to read a production AI
system as a set of contracts. Which model is pinned, which budget is enforced,
which data is trusted, which sandbox contains execution, which tenant boundary is
protected, which human gate approves side effects, which eval blocks a release,
which incident record changes the system, and which failure becomes training
signal. When those contracts are visible, the stack stops being a pile of tools
and becomes something a team can operate.

## Part reflection

- **Covered:** Model choice, serving gateways, edge deployment, fine-tuning practice, agents and sandboxes, retrieval, evaluation, observability, stack wiring, release lifecycle, reliability, human oversight, production data, and operating contracts.
- **Main concern:** Production systems fail at the joins: an unchecked model version, an unenforced budget, an unclear tenant boundary, a missing rollback path, or an incident that never becomes a regression test.
- **Takeaway:** AI infrastructure exists when SLOs, costs, approvals, data flows, incidents, and tenant boundaries are made explicit enough to operate.
- **Open question:** Which operating contracts will become standard practice as model releases, tool surfaces, and reliability expectations keep moving?
